topics.name: Rates of change and differential equations

concept_card.core_rule: Implicit differentiation finds $\frac{dy}{dx}$ when $F(x,y)=0$. Related rates use the chain rule on geometric formulas (volume/surface of cones, pyramids, spheres). First-order DEs of the forms $\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)$, $\frac{dy}{dx}=g(y)$ and $\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y)$ are solved by separation of variables. Slope fields show the direction field of a DE. Models include exponential growth/decay, logistic growth and Newton's law of cooling.

hint_levels.template: To solve a separable DE, get all the $y$'s with $dy$ on one side and all the $x$'s with $dx$ on the other, then integrate both sides.
Integrate each side, include a single constant $c$, then apply any given initial condition to find $c$.
A differential equation states a rule for how something changes; solving it recovers the quantity itself, like rebuilding a journey from a speedometer record.

worked_example.question: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx}=2xy$ with $y(0)=3$.
worked_example.explanation: Separate variables, integrate, then use the initial condition to fix the constant.

learning_objectives: Use implicit differentiation and model related-rates situations (cones, pyramids, spheres).
Solve first-order DEs $dy/dx=f(x)$, $g(y)$ and $f(x)g(y)$ by separation of variables.
Interpret slope fields and solve modelling problems including logistic growth, Newton cooling and radioactive decay.

explanation_sections.heading: Implicit differentiation and related rates
explanation_sections.body: Differentiate both sides of an implicit equation with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as $y(x)$ (so $\frac{d}{dx}[y^2]=2y\frac{dy}{dx}$), then solve for $\frac{dy}{dx}$. Related rates: write a geometric relation (e.g. $V=\frac13\pi r^2 h$ for a cone), differentiate with respect to $t$, and substitute known rates. Typical contexts: sphere $V=\frac43\pi r^3$, cone/pyramid volume and surface area. State which quantities are constant and check units.

explanation_sections.heading: Separable equations
explanation_sections.body: Three standard first-order forms: (1) $\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)$ integrate both sides; (2) $\frac{dy}{dx}=g(y)$ write $\frac{1}{g(y)}\,dy=dx$; (3) $\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y)$ separate as $\frac{1}{g(y)}\,dy=f(x)\,dx$ then integrate. Solve for $y$ where possible. Method cue: separate first, integrate second, then apply any initial condition.

explanation_sections.heading: General vs particular solutions
explanation_sections.body: Integration introduces a constant $c$ (the general solution). An initial condition such as $y(0)=3$ determines $c$, giving the particular solution. Do not apply the initial condition before integrating.

explanation_sections.heading: Slope fields
explanation_sections.body: A slope (direction/gradient) field for $\frac{dy}{dx}=F(x,y)$ draws a short segment of slope $F(x_0,y_0)$ at sample points $(x_0,y_0)$. Solution curves are tangent to these segments. Use a slope field to sketch qualitative behaviour (increasing/decreasing, equilibria) before or without solving explicitly. Technology can plot fields; you must still interpret isoclines and long-term trends.

diagram.title: Slope field for dP/dt = P(1 − P/4)

explanation_sections.heading: Growth, decay, logistic and cooling
explanation_sections.body: Exponential: $\frac{dy}{dt}=ky$ has solution $y=Ae^{kt}$ (growth if $k>0$, decay if $k<0$) — populations, radioactivity. Newton's law of cooling: $\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_a)$ so $T-T_a=Ae^{-kt}$. Logistic: $\frac{dP}{dt}=rP\bigl(1-\frac{P}{K}\bigr)$ with carrying capacity $K$; solutions approach $K$ as $t\to\infty$ for $0<P(0)<K$. Always identify parameters and check that long-term behaviour matches the model assumptions.

key_vocabulary.definition: An equation involving a function and its derivatives.
A DE that can be written so variables separate for integration.
The solution satisfying a given initial condition (no free constant).
A plot of short segments showing the slope $dy/dx$ prescribed by a DE at sample points.
A problem linking rates of change of geometric quantities through differentiation with respect to time.

common_mistakes: Forgetting the constant of integration.
Not separating the variables before integrating.
Applying the initial condition before integrating.
Treating $y$ as constant when differentiating an implicit relation with respect to $x$.
Ignoring carrying capacity or ambient temperature when interpreting logistic or cooling models.
real_world_connections: Differential equations model population dynamics, cooling, drug concentration and circuits.
Related rates connect changing dimensions to changing volume in engineering and biology.
success_criteria: I can use implicit differentiation and solve related-rates problems involving volume or surface area.
I can solve separable DEs of the forms $dy/dx=f(x)$, $g(y)$ and $f(x)g(y)$, including particular solutions.
I can interpret slope fields and model growth/decay, logistic growth and Newton cooling, checking long-term reasonableness.

concept_card.core_rule: Motion under force uses Newton's laws: resultant force equals rate of change of momentum; for constant mass, $F=ma$. Acceleration along a line may be written $\frac{dv}{dt}$, $\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$, $v\frac{dv}{dx}$ or $\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(\frac12 v^2\bigr)$. SHM satisfies $\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-\omega^2 x$ with solutions $x=A\sin(\omega t+\alpha)$ and $v^2=\omega^2(A^2-x^2)$, period $T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}$. Model vertical motion under gravity (with or without resistance) and motion on a smooth incline under concurrent forces.

hint_levels.template: Differentiate to go down the ladder (position→velocity→acceleration); integrate to go back up.
Integrate the acceleration to get velocity, using the initial velocity to fix the constant; integrate again for displacement.
Acceleration, velocity, and position are connected like a stack of odometers — each integral 'winds back' to the quantity above it.

worked_example.question: A particle has acceleration $a(t)=6t$ and starts from rest ($v(0)=0$). Find its velocity at $t=2$.
worked_example.explanation: Velocity is the integral of acceleration; the 'from rest' condition makes the constant zero. If mass is constant, the same $a(t)$ comes from $F(t)=ma(t)$.

learning_objectives: Use momentum, force and concurrent-force ideas in non-equilibrium motion.
Represent acceleration as $dv/dt$, $d^2x/dt^2$, $v\,dv/dx$ or $\frac{d}{dx}(\frac12 v^2)$ and solve straight-line problems.
Model SHM, vertical motion under gravity (with/without resistance) and smooth-incline motion.

explanation_sections.heading: Force, momentum and concurrent forces
explanation_sections.body: Momentum is $mv$. A constant force changes momentum at a constant rate; a non-constant force requires integrating $a(t)$ or using $v\frac{dv}{dx}$. Action and reaction are equal and opposite (Newton's third law). For a body under concurrent forces in non-equilibrium, resolve into components, form the resultant, and apply $F=ma$ along each axis. On a smooth incline, weight resolves into components parallel and perpendicular to the plane; the normal reaction balances the perpendicular component.

explanation_sections.heading: Acceleration forms and the kinematics ladder
explanation_sections.body: Along a straight line, acceleration may be written as $\frac{dv}{dt}$, $\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$, $v\frac{dv}{dx}$, or $\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(\frac12 v^2\bigr)$ — choose the form that matches the given data (e.g. $a$ as a function of $x$ suggests $v\frac{dv}{dx}$). Differentiate to go $x\to v\to a$; integrate to reverse, fixing constants with initial conditions. Displacement is change in position; distance adds path length including reversals.

diagram.title: Position x(t) = t² − 2t: displacement and turning point

explanation_sections.heading: Simple harmonic motion
explanation_sections.body: If $\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-\omega^2 x$, the motion is SHM about $x=0$ with angular frequency $\omega$. General solutions: $x=A\sin(\omega t+\alpha)$ or $x=A\cos(\omega t+\beta)$. Identity: $v^2=\omega^2(A^2-x^2)$. Period $T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}$ and frequency $f=\frac{1}{T}$. Amplitude $A$ is the maximum $|x|$; check energy-style consistency with $v^2=\omega^2(A^2-x^2)$.

explanation_sections.heading: Vertical motion, resistance and inclines
explanation_sections.body: Vertical motion under gravity: take upward positive so $a=-g$ without resistance; with air resistance, $a$ depends on $v$ (model as given in the problem) and integrate carefully. Smooth incline: resolve weight into $mg\sin\theta$ down the plane and $mg\cos\theta$ into the plane; no friction, so acceleration down the plane is $g\sin\theta$ when free. Exclude pulley/connected-body systems unless extended beyond the syllabus core. Vector components in 2-D still obey the same calculus ladder per component.

diagram.title: Smooth incline: weight, reaction and resolved components

key_vocabulary.definition: The vector sum of concurrent forces acting on a body; equals $ma$ for constant mass.
Motion with $\ddot x=-\omega^2 x$; oscillatory with period $2\pi/\omega$.
A known value (e.g. $v(0)$) used to determine a constant of integration.
An expression for acceleration useful when $a$ is given in terms of $x$ or $v$ along a line.

common_mistakes: Omitting the constant of integration when finding velocity or displacement.
Confusing displacement with distance travelled.
Using $a=dv/dt$ when the data are given as $a(x)$ (prefer $v\,dv/dx$).
Forgetting the negative sign in $\ddot x=-\omega^2 x$ for SHM restoring acceleration.
Resolving weight incorrectly on an incline (mixing $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$).
real_world_connections: SHM models springs, pendulums (small angle) and oscillating circuits analogues.
Incline and resistance models appear in vehicle dynamics and sports biomechanics.
success_criteria: I can relate force, momentum and acceleration and resolve concurrent forces including on a smooth incline.
I can use the acceleration forms $dv/dt$, $v\,dv/dx$ and the kinematics ladder with initial conditions.
I can model SHM and vertical motion under gravity (with or without resistance), checking period, amplitude and direction.

concept_card.core_rule: The sample mean $\bar X$ is a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard error $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ (population SD $\sigma$). For large $n$, $\bar X$ is approximately normal: $\bar X\sim N\bigl(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\bigr)$, and $\frac{\bar X-\mu}{s/\sqrt n}$ is approximately standard normal for $n\ge30$ (CLT with sample SD $s$ for moderately skewed distributions, whereas heavier-tailed distributions require larger samples). An approximate CI for $\mu$ is $\bar x\pm z\frac{s}{\sqrt n}$ with margin of error $E=z\frac{s}{\sqrt n}$; larger $n$ or smaller confidence level narrows $E$. Most but not all sample CIs contain $\mu$.

hint_levels.template: Averaging a sample reduces variability: the spread of sample means is the population spread divided by $\sqrt{n}$.

explanation_sections.heading: Sampling distribution of the mean
explanation_sections.body: Over many samples of fixed size $n$, $\bar X$ centres on $\mu$ with standard error $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$. Notation: $\bar X\sim N\bigl(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\bigr)$ when the normal model applies. By the CLT, for large $n$ (often $n\ge30$) the quantity $\frac{\bar X-\mu}{s/\sqrt n}$ is approximately standard normal even when the population is not normal, with $s$ the sample standard deviation. Check: random sample, independence, and large enough $n$ before using the normal model.

explanation_sections.heading: Repeated sampling and sample size
explanation_sections.body: The sample mean changes from sample to sample, but its long-run mean remains $\mu$. Increasing $n$ reduces its standard deviation from $\sigma$ to $\sigma/\sqrt n$ and makes the sampling distribution increasingly normal for a broad range of populations. Repeated random sampling or simulation should be used to compare different source distributions and sample sizes; the CLT concerns the distribution of sample means, not the original observations.

diagram.title: Effect of sample size on the distribution of sample means

explanation_sections.heading: Confidence intervals for a mean
explanation_sections.body: An approximate confidence interval for $\mu$ is $\bigl(\bar x-z\frac{s}{\sqrt n},\ \bar x+z\frac{s}{\sqrt n}\bigr)$, where $z$ is the standard normal quantile for the confidence level (e.g. $1.96$ for $95\%$). If $\sigma$ is known, replace $s$ by $\sigma$. Margin of error $E=z\frac{s}{\sqrt n}$. Raising confidence (larger $z$) widens $E$; raising $n$ narrows $E$ like $1/\sqrt n$. Interpretation: using this method, about $C\%$ of intervals from repeated samples would contain $\mu$ — not a probability statement about one fixed interval after the data are in. Different samples give different intervals; most contain $\mu$, some do not. Using $\bar x$ and $s$ to form a normal interval covering a desired proportion of population values is a different task from a CI for the mean $\mu$ — do not confuse the two.

key_vocabulary.definition: $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ (or $\frac{s}{\sqrt n}$ when estimated), the SD of the sample mean.
For large $n$, the sample mean is approximately normal; with $s$, $(\bar X-\mu)/(s/\sqrt n)$ is approx. $N(0,1)$ for $n\ge30$.
An interval estimate such as $\bar x\pm z s/\sqrt n$ for the population mean $\mu$.
$E=z\frac{s}{\sqrt n}$, half-width of the approximate CI for $\mu$.

common_mistakes: Using $\sigma$ instead of $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}$ for the spread of the sample mean.
Interpreting a confidence interval as a probability about a single sample mean after data are fixed.
Forgetting that larger $n$ narrows the interval.
Using $z$ with $s$ for very small $n$ without checking the large-sample condition.
Confusing a CI for $\mu$ with an interval meant to cover a proportion of individual values.
real_world_connections: Confidence intervals quantify uncertainty in polls, quality control and scientific measurement.
Sample-size planning balances cost against a target margin of error.
